fix: The popular restaurant chain confirmed on Thursday that it had taken action to address the security issue to prevent any unauthorized access to its customer database. TechCrunch withheld publication of this story until the bug was confirmed to be fixed.
impact: The exposed database contained customer names, email addresses (including whether or not the customer verified their email), dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes. The data also included veteran status, the number of times customers had logged in, when their accounts were created, and the IP addresses of their most recent log-ins, which can be used to reveal the person’s approximate location. Applebee’s had at least 8.5 million customers enrolled in its rewards program as of last year, though the company would not provide a number of how many customers had their personal information exposed by this security flaw.

fix: Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here.
impact: The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Cursor said that the malicious extension attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor using an added attacker-controlled SSH key, enabling the local SSH service, and opening a reverse SSH tunnel. Because Cursor extensions run with the permissions of the tool’s Integrated Development Environment, the backdoored version likely would gain access to local files, source code, and developer tooling once it was installed.

impact: The repository can appear in AI coding agents‘ search results, leading them to follow instructions that install remote-access malware on developers’ Windows machines and potentially expose cryptocurrency wallets stored on those systems. The README instructs AI agents to run a PowerShell command using Invoke-WebRequest and Invoke-Expression to download and execute a 21 MB dropper, indicator.ps1, directly in memory via fileless execution. The malware also adds `client32.exe` to the Windows Registry so that it starts automatically whenever the user logs in.

fix: Simply installing the latest version of the extension is not enough to clear the persistence mechanism, either. The full details of how to remediate the issue, and links to download scripts to wipe the infection, are laid out in Cursor's account of the situation.
impact: The company was forced to issue a statement after prominent figures in the cybersecurity industry alleged that the extension, which infected up to 5,000 developers, was uploaded to Cursor’s marketplace following a breach at Claudemaker Towers. According to Cursor, the extension – version 2.1.313 – was available to download for around 11 hours between 0227 and 1335 PT (0927 and 2035 UTC) on Thursday. Regardless, the extension still forwards the collected host and user data to the attacker, as well as dropping the attacker's SSH key and installing the persistence mechanism, so developers must go threat hunting in case their instance allows for the SSH tunnel to be created successfully.

impact: Check Point Research has spent two months tracking a campaign it calls Yoba, which uses the popularity of AI tools to spread a custom malware chain. The attackers build fake GitHub projects that pose as AI desktop applications such as GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus. Each ZIP holds a legitimate signed executable from OpenAI or Anthropic, named Setup.exe, next to a malicious winmm.dll.
